description: Database-backed worker backend for Django's Tasks framework (django.tasks), on Django 5.2 LTS and later. Background tasks run on the database you already have. No broker to provision or back up.
rules: Requires Python 3.12 or later and Django 5.2 or later. Django 6.0 and later ship the Tasks framework in core. On Django 5.2 LTS it comes from the django-tasks backport, so install django-ox[backport] there rather than plain django-ox.
Add django_ox to INSTALLED_APPS and set BACKEND to django_ox.backend.OxBackend in the TASKS setting.
Run python manage.py migrate django_ox before starting a worker.
Start a worker with the ox_worker management command. It is a separate process from the web server, and tasks only execute while a worker is running.

Tasks use the standard decorator and enqueue API. OxBackend also accepts provisional max_attempts, backoff and timeout fields on Django 6.1 or Django 5.2 with django-tasks 0.12+. Django 6.0 rejects policy kwargs; other backends must accept the fields.

enqueue() is one INSERT on the database the router sends OxTask to, default unless you wrote a router. A task enqueued in transaction.atomic() on that database commits or rolls back with the rows you write there. No transaction.on_commit() needed.

A bare transaction.atomic() opens on default. The joint commit needs it opened on the database OxTask routes to, and the caller's own rows written there too. Rows on another connection give two transactions, not one.
Workers claim tasks with SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on PostgreSQL and MySQL 8 or later, and with an atomic compare-and-set on databases without SKIP LOCKED, including SQLite.
django_ox.bulk.enqueue_many(task, calls) enqueues one task many times, where calls is a list of (args, kwargs) pairs. It returns TaskResult objects in input order.
enqueue_many inserts 1,000 rows per INSERT inside one transaction. Queue, priority and run_after are set once on the task with .using(...), never per call.
Execution is at-least-once, so tasks should be written to be idempotent.

Use ox_health queue thresholds for fleet alerting, not per-container liveness. --worker-timeout measures recent claims across workers, not local loop liveness. Use ox_prune to delete finished task rows older than a cutoff.
path("ox/", include("django_ox.urls")) exposes GET /ox/metrics, the queue stats as Prometheus gauges.

The /ox/metrics gauges are django_ox_tasks{queue,status}, django_ox_ready_tasks, django_ox_oldest_ready_age_seconds, django_ox_last_claim_age_seconds, django_ox_throughput_per_minute and django_ox_failure_rate.
The /ox/metrics view has no authentication; wrap it with login_required or restrict it by network. django_ox.metrics.collector() registers the same gauges with an existing prometheus_client registry.
Install with pip install django-ox. Configuration lives in the TASKS setting; the smallest working entry is TASKS = {"default": {"BACKEND": "django_ox.backend.OxBackend"}}.

Per-task policy requires Django 6.1 or Django 5.2 with django-tasks 0.12+. Django 6.0 rejects policy keywords; bare @task works. Stock test backends reject policy on fresh import or may silently ignore it after a backend switch.

The schedule and worker OPTIONS are SCHEDULES, SCHEDULE_SOURCE, SCHEDULE_RECONCILE_INTERVAL (60 seconds), SCHEDULABLE_TASKS ({}) and WORKER_CLASS, the dotted path of a django_ox.worker.Worker subclass for ox_worker to run.
QUEUES sits beside OPTIONS in the TASKS entry, not inside OPTIONS.
The row stores max_attempts at enqueue, counting the first claim. Backoff and timeout come from the worker's live task declaration on each attempt. Task.using() cannot set policy fields.
A task thread that has not stopped TASK_TIMEOUT_GRACE seconds after its deadline is recorded as failed, and the worker exits with code 75 so its supervisor restarts it.

Timeout precedence: task timeout, then TASK_TIMEOUTS[queue], then TASK_TIMEOUT. A task timeout applies even on a queue exempted with None. There is no per-task disable value. Every attempt gets a fresh timeout.

TASK_TIMEOUT bounds one attempt in seconds. At its deadline, a sync task receives TaskTimeout and an async task is cancelled, subject to the tracing exception below. django_ox.deadline() and django_ox.remaining() expose the deadline inside a task.

If a coverage tool or a debugger is watching the task thread (a sys.settrace hook, or sys.monitoring with events enabled), nothing is raised inside a sync task and the worker logs timeouts_backstop_only.

Under timeouts_backstop_only a sync task that returns within TASK_TIMEOUT_GRACE is recorded as whatever it did, and one still running then is recorded as failed and recycles the worker. An async task is cancelled at the deadline either way.

Use django_ox.testing.ImmediateBackend or DummyBackend on supported Django versions. Both validate policy, but enforce no retries, backoff or timeouts. task_policy_inert warns once per task per backend instance. Test enforcement with a real worker.

LOCK_TIMEOUT bounds how long a worker may stop refreshing its lease, not task runtime. Renewal is attempted every LOCK_TIMEOUT / 3 seconds; the lease holds only while renewal reaches the database on time.

With Django's PostgreSQL pool, renewal needs a connection. In 1.4.0 it opens one outside the pool with a bounded deadline and a short pooled fallback. Sizing LOCK_TIMEOUT alone does not prevent a reclaim.

Recurring tasks are declared in OPTIONS["SCHEDULES"] with a dotted task path and a five-field cron expression. Every running worker dispatches schedules and a unique constraint enqueues each due tick once, so there is no separate scheduler process.

OPTIONS["SCHEDULES"] takes either "cron" or "every", never both. "every" is a timedelta or a number of seconds with an optional "phase", and its ticks are counted from a fixed instant rather than from the last run, so a restart cannot shift the cadence.
Schedules can live in the database and be edited in the Django admin without a deploy: set OPTIONS["SCHEDULE_SOURCE"] to "django_ox.stored.DatabaseScheduleSource" and run migrate.

A stored schedule row names a key exposed in code with @schedulable or OPTIONS["SCHEDULABLE_TASKS"], never an import path, so admin change permission does not become permission to run any importable callable.

Write stored schedules with django_ox.stored.create_schedule and update_schedule, not OxSchedule.objects.create(): Django save() does not call full_clean(), so a direct write skips validation and leaves the activation boundary stale.

A stored schedule carries start_time as its activation boundary, set when the row is created. Retiming it reschedules from the moment of the change rather than firing a tick that already passed under the old timing.

Re-enabling a paused stored schedule does not replay the ticks it missed; there is no backfill. Kubernetes schedules a CronJob's missed Jobs on unsuspend when no starting deadline is set, and Quartz applies the misfire instruction on resume.
starting_deadline_seconds on a stored schedule drops a tick later than that rather than running it however stale, and logs schedule_tick_dropped with its lateness. The default is no deadline.
A recurring tick enqueues an ordinary task, so execution stays at-least-once: a tick enqueued once can still run more than once and should be idempotent.

After an outage only the most recent missed tick is enqueued and older ones are skipped, and a new schedule never fires for a time before it existed, so some cron occurrences are deliberately never enqueued.
The task function is called outside any transaction. A task that needs select_for_update() or atomic writes opens its own transaction.atomic().

ox_worker --concurrency N is a thread pool inside one process. ox_worker --processes N runs N worker processes under one supervisor, each with its own database connections. For CPU-bound tasks use --processes N --concurrency 1.
A worker process that dies is restarted after one second, doubling to 30 seconds. More than five deaths of one slot within a minute stops the supervisor with exit code 1.
django_ox.actions.retry(result_id) requeues a FAILED or LOST task for one more attempt. django_ox.actions.discard(result_id) closes a READY, WAITING, FAILED or LOST task without running it.

Budget concurrency + 1 pooled connections per worker, plus 2 unpooled as a worst case: renewal and a possible timeout watchdog. Task-declared timeouts count. This is capacity guidance, not a count of open connections or a startup requirement.

OPTIONS defaults: MAX_ATTEMPTS=3, LOCK_TIMEOUT=300, BACKOFF_INITIAL=5, BACKOFF_MAX=600, TASK_TIMEOUT=None, TASK_TIMEOUTS={}, TASK_TIMEOUT_GRACE=30. Durations are in seconds; MAX_ATTEMPTS counts claims, including the first.

Without a task backoff callback, retry delay after attempt n is min(BACKOFF_INITIAL * 2 ** (n - 1), BACKOFF_MAX), with no jitter. Invalid callback results or worker-side callback failures use this fallback; returning None stops retries.

OxTask.Status.WAITING is a status django-ox never writes itself. Workers never claim a waiting task, ox_prune never deletes it, and retry skips it. It reads as READY through django.tasks. Workflows in Oxpull Pro write and release it.
ox_worker, ox_prune and database-mode ox_health take --database; it defaults to the OxTask write alias and is not checked against the router. ox_health --heartbeat-file refuses --database.

ox_import_beat_schedules takes --database too, but it names a different thing: the alias holding your django-celery-beat tables. It defaults to the alias the router sends OxSchedule reads to. The command writes nothing anywhere.

django-ox is finite on purpose: a durable queue, a worker, recurring schedules and monitoring, including django_ox.stats and ox_health. Batches, unique tasks, rate limiting and workflows live in Oxpull Pro, a paid add-on at oxpull.com.

For optional local liveness, pair ox_worker --heartbeat-file PATH with ox_health --heartbeat-file PATH and matching --processes N. A pass means the expected controlling loops have advanced recently, not task progress. A hung DB can cause restart storms.
